title: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN): A Framework for Overlaying Virtualized Layer 2 Networks over Layer 3 Networks
summary: This document describes VXLAN, a scheme for building overlay networks that carry virtualized Layer 2 networks over Layer 3 networks. It addresses multi-tenant needs in cloud and enterprise data centers, and documents the deployed protocol for the Internet community.

plainLanguage.summary: VXLAN carries an Ethernet frame inside an outer packet so it can cross an IP network. A VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) keeps each virtual network separate, even when different segments use the same MAC addresses. The RFC documents this deployed protocol.

subtitle: VXLAN carries virtual Ethernet frames across an IP network using a segment identifier.

tldr.problem: Virtualized data centers need isolated Layer 2 networks across shared infrastructure. The RFC describes pressures from the VLAN limit, overlapping tenant addresses, large MAC tables, and Layer 2 links disabled by Spanning Tree.
tldr.mechanism: VXLAN places an 8-byte header and outer UDP/IP headers around an Ethernet frame. A 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) selects the overlay segment, while tunnel endpoints add and remove the outer headers.
tldr.outcome: The document records the deployed VXLAN protocol for the Internet community. It is an Informational RFC, not an Internet Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 7348 is an Informational document that records the deployed VXLAN protocol. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Data Centers Need an Overlay
sections.content:
Virtualization places many virtual machines, each with its own MAC address, on physical servers. This increases the number of addresses that top-of-rack switches must learn, and a full table can lead to flooding of frames with unknown destinations.

The RFC also describes pressure on the 4094-VLAN limit, tenant networks that may reuse addresses, and links blocked by Spanning Tree. VXLAN carries Layer 2 traffic over Layer 3 while preserving separation between virtual networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Many virtual machines share the same physical network, but each tenant needs an isolated network. VXLAN carries those separate Layer 2 networks across an IP network.

sections.title: Segments and Tunnel Endpoints
sections.content:
Each VXLAN overlay is a segment identified by a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI). Only virtual machines in the same segment communicate through that overlay, so different segments can use overlapping MAC addresses.

A VXLAN Tunnel End Point (VTEP) encapsulates a VM's Ethernet frame and sends it toward a remote VTEP. The receiving VTEP checks the VNI, removes the outer headers, and passes the original frame to the destination VM. The RFC focuses on learning MAC-to-VTEP mappings from traffic; it also notes that directory-based approaches are possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The VNI tells a VTEP which virtual network carries a frame. The far VTEP removes the added headers and delivers the original Ethernet frame to the VM.

sections.title: Unicast, Broadcast, and the Physical Network
sections.content:
For known unicast traffic, a VTEP looks up the destination MAC address and sends the encapsulated frame to the remote VTEP. The receiving VTEP learns the mapping from the inner source MAC address to the outer source IP address.

For broadcasts, unknown destinations, and multicast frames, the RFC describes mapping each VNI to an IP multicast group. VTEPs join groups using IGMP. VTEPs must not fragment VXLAN packets; the RFC recommends that the physical network MTU accommodate the larger encapsulated frame.
sections.plainLanguage: A VTEP sends known traffic to the VTEP serving its destination. It sends broadcast and unknown-destination traffic to the multicast group associated with the segment.

sections.title: The VXLAN Packet
sections.content:
The original Ethernet frame is carried inside an outer Ethernet, IP, UDP, and VXLAN header. The VXLAN header is 8 bytes: an 8-bit flags field, a 24-bit VNI, and reserved fields of 24 and 8 bits.

The I flag must be set for a valid VNI. Reserved fields must be zero when sent and are ignored when received. UDP destination port 4789 is assigned for VXLAN and should be the default; the RFC recommends a source port derived from a hash of inner-packet fields to support equal-cost multipath load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer headers carry the VM's original Ethernet frame across the physical network. The VXLAN header marks which segment the frame belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encapsulating Layer 2 traffic over IP expands the attack surface. An unauthorized endpoint could join a multicast group or inject MAC-over-UDP frames, potentially adding false traffic or taking over a MAC address.

The RFC does not build specific protections into VXLAN. It describes measures such as restricting who can manage VMs and gateways, using access controls, protecting tunnel traffic with IPsec, and securely communicating VNI and VM membership mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: VXLAN itself does not stop an unauthorized device from sending false traffic. The RFC points to network access controls and protection for tunneled traffic as possible safeguards.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The I flag is set for a valid VNI; other bits are reserved.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission; ignored on receipt.
